questions.expected: To preserve them for future generations and keep them as attractions
questions.memo: Protecting heritage keeps it intact for future generations and maintains the sites that draw cultural and heritage tourists.

questions.question: Sort each item by whether it is protected heritage.
questions.memo: Old structures, shipwrecks, meteorites and burial grounds are protected heritage. New, everyday buildings and objects are not.

questions.question: Which of these is protected under South African heritage rules?
questions.memo: Meteorites are protected heritage materials and may not be collected or sold without the correct permits.

questions.question: True or false: SAHRA is a national body that works across the whole of South Africa.
questions.memo: SAHRA operates at national level, while provincial heritage agencies handle heritage within each province.

questions.question: Before altering a protected heritage site, a person must first obtain a heritage _________.
questions.memo: A heritage permit gives official permission to alter, move or work on a protected site, ensuring the heritage is properly managed.

questions.question: What can happen if someone damages protected heritage without a permit?
options: It is illegal and they can face penalties
Nothing, because heritage is not protected
They automatically become the site's owner
They receive a reward from SAHRA
questions.expected: It is illegal and they can face penalties
questions.memo: Damaging protected heritage without permission breaks the law and can lead to fines or other penalties.

questions.question: Which action would require a heritage permit?
options: Demolishing a building that is more than 60 years old
Painting your own new garden fence
Buying a souvenir from a shop
questions.expected: Demolishing a building that is more than 60 years old
questions.memo: Because structures older than 60 years are protected, demolishing one requires a permit. Ordinary modern activities do not.

questions.question: Sort each responsibility by whether it belongs to the national body (SAHRA) or to a provincial heritage agency.

items.text: Protecting heritage across the whole country
Managing heritage within a single province
Issuing permits for sites in that province

questions.memo: SAHRA works at national level (national policy and protection); provincial agencies handle heritage matters within their own province.

questions.question: True or false: Burial grounds and graves are protected heritage in South Africa.
questions.memo: Burial grounds and graves are protected, and permits are needed before they may be disturbed or relocated.

questions.question: How does protecting heritage support tourism?
options: It keeps important sites intact so tourists can keep visiting them
It closes all attractions to visitors
It removes the reasons for tourists to come
It has no link to tourism at all
questions.expected: It keeps important sites intact so tourists can keep visiting them
questions.memo: Well-protected heritage sites remain attractive and authentic, so they continue to draw cultural and heritage tourists.

questions.question: What is the difference between an archaeological site and a palaeontological site?
options: Archaeological sites hold human-made remains; palaeontological sites hold fossils of ancient life
They are exactly the same thing
Archaeological sites hold fossils; palaeontological sites hold modern litter
questions.expected: Archaeological sites hold human-made remains; palaeontological sites hold fossils of ancient life
questions.memo: Archaeology deals with human-made artefacts and remains; palaeontology deals with fossils of ancient plants and animals. Both are protected.

questions.question: _________ wrecks lying under the sea are protected heritage and may not be disturbed without a permit.
questions.memo: Shipwrecks are protected heritage, often holding historical value, so permits are required before they may be explored or removed.

TOUR.G11.T2.FOREX.A1.title: Foreign exchange and its value to the economy
TOUR.G11.T2.FOREX.A1.description: Use foreign-exchange concepts (local currency, foreign currency, exchange rate, fluctuations), recognise major world currencies, their codes and symbols, where currency is exchanged, and explain how spending by inbound tourists benefits locals directly and indirectly through the multiplier effect.
TOUR.G11.T2.FOREX.A1.strand: Term 2 — Domestic growth, culture and foreign exchange
TOUR.G11.T2.FOREX.A1.caps_topic: Foreign exchange — foreign exchange and its value to the South African economy
TOUR.G11.T2.FOREX.A1.recovery_strategy: Trace one tourist's rand from the hotel to the supplier to the worker, then match currencies to their codes.

questions.question: What is foreign exchange?
options: Exchanging the money of one country for the money of another
Sending a letter to another country
questions.expected: Exchanging the money of one country for the money of another
questions.memo: Foreign exchange means swapping one currency for another — for example a tourist changing US dollars into South African rand.

questions.question: What is an exchange rate?
options: The price of one currency expressed in terms of another
The speed at which money is spent
The fee charged to enter a country
The number of tourists in a country
questions.expected: The price of one currency expressed in terms of another
questions.memo: An exchange rate tells you how much of one currency you get for another — for example how many rand one US dollar is worth.

questions.question: South Africa's local currency is the _________.
questions.memo: The rand (ZAR, symbol R) is South Africa's local currency. Foreign currencies are those of other countries.

questions.question: True or false: Exchange rates can change (fluctuate) from day to day.
questions.memo: Exchange rates fluctuate constantly because of supply, demand and economic conditions, so the rand's value against other currencies changes over time.

questions.question: Which currency code and symbol belong to the United States dollar?
questions.memo: The US dollar uses the code USD and the symbol $. GBP/£ is the pound, EUR/€ the euro and JPY/¥ the yen.

questions.question: What is the multiplier effect in tourism?
options: Money spent by tourists is re-spent again and again, benefiting many people
Tourists multiply the number of flights they take
Hotels multiply their room prices each year
The number of tourists doubles every month
questions.expected: Money spent by tourists is re-spent again and again, benefiting many people
questions.memo: The multiplier effect means one tourist's spending passes from business to supplier to worker, so the money circulates and benefits many people, not just the first business.

questions.question: Inbound international tourists bring _________ currency into South Africa when they spend here.
questions.memo: Inbound tourists exchange their foreign currency to spend in South Africa, bringing valuable foreign earnings into the economy.

questions.question: True or false: The money a foreign tourist spends only ever benefits the hotel they stay in.
questions.memo: Through the multiplier effect, the tourist's money spreads from the hotel to its suppliers, staff and beyond, benefiting many people in the economy.

questions.question: Where can a foreign tourist exchange currency in South Africa?
options: At a foreign exchange bureau or a commercial bank
At a petrol station fuel pump
questions.expected: At a foreign exchange bureau or a commercial bank
questions.memo: Foreign exchange bureaus and commercial banks are the usual places to change one currency into another.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by choosing the strong supporting points.
questions.thesis: Money spent by inbound international tourists is valuable to South Africa's economy.

pool.text: It brings foreign currency into the country
It creates and supports jobs in many tourism businesses
Through the multiplier effect it circulates and benefits many people

questions.memo: The strong points link tourist spending to foreign earnings, jobs and money circulating through the economy. The red herrings are true but do not support the economic value.

questions.question: Which is an example of a DIRECT benefit of tourist spending?
options: A hotel earns money when a tourist pays for a room
A farmer sells more vegetables to the hotel's supplier
A taxi driver's spending supports a local shop
A builder is hired because the area is growing
questions.expected: A hotel earns money when a tourist pays for a room
questions.memo: A direct benefit is the first payment from the tourist (the hotel room). Indirect benefits happen later as that money is re-spent through the economy.

questions.question: The British _________ is one of the major currencies of the world.
questions.memo: The British pound (GBP, £) is a major world currency, along with the US dollar, euro, yen, Australian dollar and South African rand.

questions.question: True or false: The euro is the currency used by many European countries.
questions.memo: The euro (EUR, €) is shared by many European countries, making it one of the world's major currencies.

questions.question: Which symbol represents the British pound?
questions.memo: The pound's symbol is £. The dollar is $, the euro is € and the yen is ¥.

questions.question: Match each currency to its country or region.
questions.memo: The US dollar ($) is from the United States, the pound (£) from the United Kingdom and the yen (¥) from Japan.

questions.question: How does foreign exchange from tourism add value to the South African economy?
options: It brings in foreign earnings and supports jobs and businesses
It removes money from the country
It has no effect on local people
questions.expected: It brings in foreign earnings and supports jobs and businesses
questions.memo: Foreign currency spent by tourists is earned by the country, supporting jobs, businesses and government income.

questions.question: True or false: A bureau de change (foreign exchange bureau) is a place where travellers can change one currency into another.
questions.memo: A foreign exchange bureau exists specifically to exchange currencies for travellers, alongside commercial banks.

questions.question: Sort each outcome by whether it is a direct or an indirect benefit of tourist spending.

items.text: A tourist pays a restaurant for a meal
The restaurant then buys more food from a local farmer
A tourist pays for a guided tour
The guide spends their wages at local shops
A tourist pays a hotel for a room

questions.memo: Direct benefits are the tourist's first payments. Indirect benefits happen as that money is re-spent (the multiplier effect).

questions.question: Which symbol represents the Japanese yen?
questions.memo: The yen's symbol is ¥. The pound is £, the dollar $ and the euro €.

questions.question: Foreign _________ earned from inbound tourists helps strengthen South Africa's economy.
questions.memo: Foreign exchange (foreign currency earned from tourists) brings money into the country and supports the economy.

TOUR.G11.T2.CURRENCY.A1.title: Conversion of currencies
TOUR.G11.T2.CURRENCY.A1.description: Read a currency rate sheet from a foreign-exchange bureau and convert major currencies to South African rand and rand into a chosen currency, rounding to two decimals.
TOUR.G11.T2.CURRENCY.A1.strand: Term 2 — Domestic growth, culture and foreign exchange
TOUR.G11.T2.CURRENCY.A1.recovery_strategy: Fix the rule 'rand to foreign = divide by the rate; foreign to rand = multiply by the rate', then practise one conversion at a time.

questions.question: The rate is 1 USD = R18,00. How many rand will a tourist get for US$100?
questions.memo: To change a foreign currency into rand, multiply by the rate: 100 × R18,00 = R1 800,00.

questions.question: The rate is 1 USD = R18,00. How many US dollars will R3 600 buy?
questions.memo: To change rand into a foreign currency, divide by the rate: R3 600 ÷ 18 = $200,00.

questions.question: To change rand into a foreign currency, you _________ the rand amount by the exchange rate.
questions.memo: Rand to foreign currency: divide by the rate. Foreign currency to rand: multiply by the rate.

questions.question: True or false: A currency rate sheet shows how many rand one unit of a foreign currency is worth.
questions.memo: A rate sheet lists the exchange rates, for example 1 USD = R18,00, telling you the rand value of each foreign currency.

questions.question: The rate is 1 GBP = R23,00. Convert £50 into rand.
questions.memo: Foreign to rand: multiply by the rate. 50 × R23,00 = R1 150,00.

questions.question: The rate is 1 EUR = R20,00. Convert €200 into rand.
questions.memo: Foreign to rand: multiply by the rate. 200 × R20,00 = R4 000,00.

questions.question: To change a foreign currency into rand, you _________ the amount by the exchange rate.
questions.memo: Foreign currency to rand: multiply by the rate. Rand to foreign currency: divide by the rate.

questions.question: True or false: When rounding to two decimals, R34,567 becomes R34,57.
questions.memo: Rounding R34,567 to two decimals: the third digit (7) rounds the second decimal up, giving R34,57.

questions.question: The rate is 1 GBP = R23,00. How many pounds will R4 600 buy?
questions.memo: Rand to foreign: divide by the rate. R4 600 ÷ 23 = £200,00.

questions.question: Sort each conversion by whether you multiply or divide by the exchange rate.
questions.memo: Foreign currency to rand = multiply by the rate. Rand to foreign currency = divide by the rate.

questions.question: The rate is 1 USD = R18,00. Convert US$250 into rand.
questions.memo: Foreign to rand: multiply by the rate. 250 × R18,00 = R4 500,00.

questions.question: True or false: The same exchange rate can be used to convert money in both directions (rand to foreign, and foreign to rand).
questions.memo: One rate can be used both ways: multiply to go from foreign currency to rand, and divide to go from rand to foreign currency.

questions.question: Rounded to two decimal places, R12,3456 becomes R12,_________.
questions.memo: The third decimal (5) rounds the second decimal up, so R12,3456 becomes R12,35.

questions.question: The rate is 1 USD = R18,00. How many US dollars will R1 000 buy (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.memo: Rand to foreign: divide by the rate. R1 000 ÷ 18 = $55,555… which rounds to $55,56.

questions.question: The rate is 1 EUR = R20,00. A tourist has €500. How many rand is this?
questions.memo: Foreign to rand: multiply by the rate. 500 × R20,00 = R10 000,00.

questions.question: Sort each task by the conversion direction.

items.text: A British tourist changes pounds to spend in Cape Town
A South African buys dollars before flying to New York
A Japanese visitor changes yen on arrival in Durban
A South African buys euros for a trip to Paris
A German tourist changes euros to rand

questions.memo: Foreigners arriving in South Africa change their currency to rand (multiply). South Africans going abroad buy foreign currency with rand (divide).

questions.question: True or false: When the rand is weak, a tourist needs more rand to buy one US dollar.
questions.memo: A weak rand means each dollar costs more rand, so it takes more rand to buy the same foreign currency.

questions.question: The rate is 1 USD = R18,00. Convert US$80 into rand.
questions.memo: Foreign to rand: multiply by the rate. 80 × R18,00 = R1 440,00.

questions.question: Which is the correct method to convert rand into euros?
options: Divide the rand amount by the exchange rate
Multiply the rand amount by the exchange rate
Add the exchange rate to the rand amount
Subtract the exchange rate from the rand amount
questions.expected: Divide the rand amount by the exchange rate
questions.memo: To go from rand to a foreign currency such as euros, divide the rand amount by the rate.

questions.question: When doing currency conversions, money amounts are usually rounded to _________ decimal places.
questions.memo: Currency amounts are rounded to two decimal places, for example R34,56, because money is counted in cents.

TOUR.G11.T3.SADC.A1.title: Regional tourism and the SADC member countries
TOUR.G11.T3.SADC.A1.description: Explain regional tourism and the Southern African Development Community (SADC), locate member countries and their capitals, describe how each is reached from South Africa (gateways: road, air, water), the role of Retosa, and the advantages of regional tourism.
TOUR.G11.T3.SADC.A1.strand: Term 3 — Regional tourism, itineraries and marketing
TOUR.G11.T3.SADC.A1.caps_topic: Domestic, regional and international tourism — regional tourism and the SADC member countries
TOUR.G11.T3.SADC.A1.recovery_strategy: Match each member country to its capital and main gateway, one country at a time.

questions.question: What is regional tourism?
options: Travel between countries in the same region, such as Southern Africa
Travel that never crosses a border
questions.expected: Travel between countries in the same region, such as Southern Africa
questions.memo: Regional tourism is travel between countries that are close together in the same region — for South Africa, this means the SADC countries.

questions.question: What does SADC stand for?
questions.memo: SADC is the Southern African Development Community, a group of Southern African countries that cooperate on development, including tourism.

questions.question: The capital city of Botswana is _________.
questions.memo: Gaborone is the capital of Botswana. Windhoek is Namibia's, Harare is Zimbabwe's and Lusaka is Zambia's.

questions.question: True or false: Lesotho is a landlocked country completely surrounded by South Africa.
questions.memo: Lesotho is fully surrounded by South Africa and has no coastline, so it is reached overland from South Africa.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Namibia?
questions.memo: Windhoek is Namibia's capital. Gaborone is in Botswana, Maputo in Mozambique and Maseru in Lesotho.

questions.question: In tourism, what is a 'gateway' to a country?
options: A main entry point such as an airport, harbour or border post
A fence around a game reserve
questions.expected: A main entry point such as an airport, harbour or border post
questions.memo: A gateway is a main way into a country — its major airport, harbour or border post — through which tourists arrive.

questions.question: Retosa was set up to promote _________ tourism in Southern Africa.
questions.memo: Retosa, the Regional Tourism Organisation of Southern Africa, was created to market and promote the region as a tourism destination.

questions.question: True or false: Zimbabwe is a member of the SADC.
questions.memo: Zimbabwe is a SADC member, along with countries such as Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and Mozambique.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Zimbabwe?
questions.memo: Harare is Zimbabwe's capital. Lusaka is in Zambia, Windhoek in Namibia and Lilongwe in Malawi.

questions.question: Match each SADC country to its capital city.
questions.memo: Gaborone is the capital of Botswana, Maputo of Mozambique and Lusaka of Zambia.

questions.question: What is one advantage of regional tourism for South Africa and its neighbours?
options: Countries can market the region together and make travel between them easier
It stops people from crossing any borders
It closes airports in the region
questions.expected: Countries can market the region together and make travel between them easier
questions.memo: Regional tourism lets neighbouring countries promote the region jointly, ease cross-border travel and share the economic benefits.

questions.question: True or false: Kenya is a member of the SADC.
questions.memo: Kenya is in East Africa and is not a SADC member. SADC members include countries such as Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

questions.question: A border _________ is where travellers cross by road from one country into another.
questions.memo: A border post is the official crossing point between countries by road, where travel documents are checked.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Mozambique?
questions.memo: Maputo is the capital of Mozambique. Maseru is in Lesotho, Lilongwe in Malawi and Luanda in Angola.

questions.question: What is the usual way for a South African tourist to reach an island country like Mauritius or the Seychelles?
questions.memo: Island countries such as Mauritius and the Seychelles are reached by air, since there is no road or rail link across the sea.

questions.question: Sort each country by whether it is a SADC member.
questions.memo: Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe are SADC members. Nigeria (West Africa) and Egypt (North Africa) are not.

questions.question: True or false: Retosa stands for the Regional Tourism Organisation of Southern Africa.
questions.memo: Retosa is the Regional Tourism Organisation of Southern Africa, which promotes the region as a single tourism destination.

questions.question: How does cooperation between SADC countries help tourism?
options: It allows joint marketing and smoother cross-border travel, attracting more visitors
It makes it harder to travel between countries
It stops tourists from visiting the region
It removes all airports and harbours
questions.expected: It allows joint marketing and smoother cross-border travel, attracting more visitors
questions.memo: Working together, SADC countries can promote the region as one destination and make it easier for tourists to travel between them.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Zambia?
questions.memo: Lusaka is Zambia's capital. Harare is in Zimbabwe, Gaborone in Botswana and Maputo in Mozambique.

questions.question: The capital city of Lesotho is _________.
questions.memo: Maseru is the capital of Lesotho. Mbabane is in Eswatini, Maputo in Mozambique and Lilongwe in Malawi.

TOUR.G11.T3.SADCATTR.A1.title: Main tourist attractions in the SADC countries
TOUR.G11.T3.SADCATTR.A1.description: Identify the main tourist attractions in the SADC countries (e.g. Okavango Delta, Victoria Falls, Mount Kilimanjaro, the Serengeti, Fish River Canyon, the Great Zimbabwe Ruins), the country each is in, and why each is a top attraction.
TOUR.G11.T3.SADCATTR.A1.strand: Term 3 — Regional tourism, itineraries and marketing
TOUR.G11.T3.SADCATTR.A1.caps_topic: Tourism attractions — main tourist attractions in the SADC countries
TOUR.G11.T3.SADCATTR.A1.recovery_strategy: Match each attraction to its country and one reason it draws tourists, one at a time.

questions.question: In which country is the Okavango Delta?
questions.memo: The Okavango Delta, a vast inland wetland rich in wildlife, is in Botswana and is one of Africa's most famous natural attractions.

questions.question: In which country is Mount Kilimanjaro?
questions.memo: Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, is in Tanzania and draws climbers and tourists from around the world.

questions.question: Victoria Falls lies on the _________ River.
questions.memo: Victoria Falls is on the Zambezi River, on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe.

questions.question: True or false: The Serengeti National Park is in Tanzania.
questions.memo: The Serengeti, famous for its great wildlife migration, is in Tanzania.

questions.question: In which country is the Fish River Canyon?
questions.memo: The Fish River Canyon, one of the largest canyons in the world, is in Namibia.

questions.question: In which country are the Great Zimbabwe Ruins?
questions.memo: The Great Zimbabwe Ruins, an ancient stone city, are in Zimbabwe and gave the country its name.

questions.question: Etosha National Park, famous for its salt pan and game viewing, is in _________.
questions.memo: Etosha National Park, built around a huge salt pan, is one of Namibia's top wildlife attractions.

questions.question: True or false: Lake Malawi is found in Malawi.
questions.memo: Lake Malawi, a large freshwater lake popular for water activities, is in Malawi.

questions.question: The Namib Desert and the Skeleton Coast are major attractions in which country?
questions.memo: The Namib Desert and the rugged Skeleton Coast are both in Namibia.

questions.question: Match each attraction to its country.
questions.memo: The Okavango Delta and Chobe are in Botswana; the Fish River Canyon and Etosha in Namibia; the Serengeti and Kilimanjaro in Tanzania.

questions.question: Chobe National Park, known for its large elephant herds, is in which country?
questions.memo: Chobe National Park in Botswana is famous for its very large elephant population.

questions.question: True or false: Victoria Falls lies on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
questions.memo: Victoria Falls is shared by Zambia and Zimbabwe, both of which use it as a major tourist attraction.

questions.question: The Bazaruto _________ is a group of islands and a popular attraction in Mozambique.
questions.memo: The Bazaruto Archipelago is a chain of islands off Mozambique, known for its beaches, diving and marine life.

questions.question: The Sani Pass and the Maluti Mountains are attractions in which country?
questions.memo: The Sani Pass and the Maluti Mountains are in Lesotho, a mountainous country surrounded by South Africa.

questions.question: Why is the Okavango Delta considered a top tourist attraction?
options: It is a unique inland wetland teeming with wildlife
It is the busiest airport in Africa
It is a large shopping centre
It is a major harbour for cruise ships
questions.expected: It is a unique inland wetland teeming with wildlife
questions.memo: The Okavango Delta is a rare inland water system rich in wildlife, offering world-class safaris and birdwatching.

questions.question: Sort each attraction by its country.
questions.memo: The Great Zimbabwe Ruins and Hwange are in Zimbabwe; the Bazaruto Archipelago and Island of Mozambique in Mozambique; the Sani Pass and Katse Dam in Lesotho.

questions.question: True or false: Mauritius is well known for its beaches and leisure activities on the islands.
questions.memo: Mauritius is a popular island destination famous for its beaches, clear waters and resort holidays.

questions.question: The Ngorongoro Conservation Area is a famous attraction in which country?
questions.memo: The Ngorongoro Conservation Area, with its huge crater full of wildlife, is in Tanzania.

questions.question: Hwange National Park is found in which country?
questions.memo: Hwange National Park, Zimbabwe's largest game reserve, is known for its elephants and varied wildlife.

questions.question: Mount _________, in Tanzania, is the highest mountain in Africa.
questions.memo: Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania is Africa's highest peak and a world-famous attraction for climbers.

TOUR.G11.T3.ITINERARY.A1.title: The tour itinerary
TOUR.G11.T3.ITINERARY.A1.description: Use itinerary concepts (itinerary, logical tour planning, scheduled tours), apply the factors to consider when planning an itinerary, recognise different types of itineraries, and judge the logical spread and appropriateness of a day-by-day plan.
TOUR.G11.T3.ITINERARY.A1.strand: Term 3 — Regional tourism, itineraries and marketing
TOUR.G11.T3.ITINERARY.A1.caps_topic: Map work and tour planning — the tour itinerary
TOUR.G11.T3.ITINERARY.A1.recovery_strategy: Plot stops on a map to show the logical order, then check a plan against the planning factors one by one.

questions.question: What is a tour itinerary?
options: A planned, day-by-day schedule of a trip's travel, stops and activities
questions.expected: A planned, day-by-day schedule of a trip's travel, stops and activities
questions.memo: An itinerary sets out the plan for a trip day by day — where the traveller goes, how they get there, where they stay and what they do.

questions.question: What does 'logical tour planning' mean?
options: Arranging stops in a sensible order that avoids unnecessary backtracking
Visiting places in a random order
Driving as far as possible every single day
Planning only the first day of the trip
questions.expected: Arranging stops in a sensible order that avoids unnecessary backtracking
questions.memo: Logical planning means ordering stops so the route flows sensibly, saving time and travel by not crisscrossing back and forth.

questions.question: A _________ tour runs on fixed dates that are set and advertised in advance.
questions.memo: Scheduled tours depart on set, pre-arranged dates, so travellers can book a place on a fixed programme.

questions.question: True or false: A well-planned itinerary avoids unnecessary backtracking.
questions.memo: Backtracking wastes time and money. A good itinerary flows logically from one stop to the next.

questions.question: Which is an important factor to consider when planning an itinerary?
options: The distance and travel time between stops
The favourite colour of the bus driver
The brand of the traveller's phone
The number of letters in each place name
questions.expected: The distance and travel time between stops
questions.memo: Distance and travel time are key, so the day is not spent entirely travelling and there is enough time at each stop.

questions.question: What makes an itinerary well balanced?
options: A good variety of activities with time to rest
Doing the exact same activity every day
Packing in so much that there is no rest
questions.expected: A good variety of activities with time to rest
questions.memo: A balanced itinerary offers variety and includes rest time, so travellers stay interested and do not become exhausted.

questions.question: A good itinerary has a logical _________ of activities across the days, not everything crammed into one day.
questions.memo: A logical spread means activities are sensibly distributed across the trip, so each day is varied and manageable.

questions.question: True or false: An itinerary lists only the hotel name and nothing else.
questions.memo: An itinerary covers each day's transport, accommodation, attractions and activities — not just the hotel.

questions.question: Which of these is a factor to consider when planning an itinerary?
options: The colour of the road signs
The number of clouds in the sky
questions.memo: Budget shapes the whole plan — the transport, accommodation and activities must fit what the traveller can afford.

questions.question: Put these South African stops in a logical west-to-east order for a coastal road trip.
questions.memo: Travelling east along the coast, the logical order is Cape Town, then Mossel Bay, then Gqeberha, then East London — no backtracking.

questions.question: What is one difference between types of itineraries?
options: Some are detailed day-by-day plans, while others give only a broad outline
All itineraries must be exactly one page long
An itinerary can only ever cover one day
Itineraries may not include any activities
questions.expected: Some are detailed day-by-day plans, while others give only a broad outline
questions.memo: Itineraries vary in detail — from a full day-by-day breakdown to a simple outline of the main stops.

questions.question: True or false: Scheduled tours have set departure dates that travellers book onto.
questions.memo: Scheduled tours run on fixed, advertised dates, so travellers join a pre-planned programme.

questions.question: A day-by-day itinerary usually shows the _________, transport, accommodation and activities for each part of the trip.
questions.memo: A day-by-day itinerary is organised by day, listing what happens each day: transport, accommodation, attractions and activities.

questions.question: Why should a planner consider the tourists' interests when writing an itinerary?
options: So the activities suit what the travellers actually want to do and enjoy
So the trip is as tiring as possible
So the planner can ignore the budget
questions.expected: So the activities suit what the travellers actually want to do and enjoy
questions.memo: Matching activities to the travellers' interests makes the trip enjoyable and appropriate for the group.

questions.question: Which is a sign of a poorly planned itinerary?
options: Long hours of driving with no time to rest or enjoy attractions
A sensible balance of travel, sightseeing and rest
Stops arranged in a logical order
Activities matched to the travellers' interests
questions.expected: Long hours of driving with no time to rest or enjoy attractions
questions.memo: Cramming in too much travel with no rest is a clear sign of poor planning; a good itinerary is balanced and realistic.

questions.question: Sort each feature by whether it shows good or poor itinerary planning.

items.text: Too many activities crammed into one day
Driving 10 hours with nothing to see

questions.memo: Good planning is logical, varied and realistic with rest. Poor planning backtracks, overloads days and wastes time travelling.

questions.question: True or false: The season and weather are factors to consider when planning an itinerary.
questions.memo: Weather and season affect what activities are possible and enjoyable, so they must be considered when planning.

questions.question: Why must a planner check the opening times of attractions?
options: So the group does not arrive when an attraction is closed
So the trip costs more money
So the bus uses more fuel
So the itinerary is harder to read
questions.expected: So the group does not arrive when an attraction is closed
questions.memo: Checking opening times avoids wasted trips to closed attractions and keeps the day running smoothly.

questions.question: Match each detail to the itinerary column it belongs in.

items.text: Fly from Johannesburg to Cape Town

questions.memo: Transport covers how you travel; accommodation is where you stay; activities are what you do at each stop.

questions.question: An itinerary that keeps crossing back and forth across an area mainly wastes _________.
questions.memo: Backtracking wastes time (and money on extra travel), which is why a logical, flowing route is so important.

TOUR.G11.T3.PROMO.A1.title: Promotional and advertising techniques
TOUR.G11.T3.PROMO.A1.description: Tell above-the-line techniques (TV, radio, newspapers, magazines, billboards, web advertising) apart from below-the-line techniques (personal selling, sales promotions, in-store discounts, sponsorship, exhibitions and expos), and match a technique to the right customer.
TOUR.G11.T3.PROMO.A1.strand: Term 3 — Regional tourism, itineraries and marketing
TOUR.G11.T3.PROMO.A1.recovery_strategy: Use the rule 'above-the-line = mass media; below-the-line = direct/targeted', then sort one technique at a time.

questions.question: What is above-the-line advertising?
options: Advertising through mass media that reaches a large, general audience
Selling face-to-face to one customer at a time
questions.expected: Advertising through mass media that reaches a large, general audience
questions.memo: Above-the-line uses mass media — TV, radio, newspapers, billboards, web adverts — to reach a wide, general audience.

questions.question: What is below-the-line promotion?
options: Direct, targeted methods such as personal selling and sales promotions
A television advert seen by millions
A billboard next to the highway
questions.expected: Direct, targeted methods such as personal selling and sales promotions
questions.memo: Below-the-line uses direct, targeted methods — personal selling, sales promotions, discounts, sponsorship and expos — aimed at specific customers.

questions.question: A television advert is an _________-the-line technique.
questions.memo: Television reaches a large general audience through mass media, making it an above-the-line technique.

questions.question: True or false: Personal selling is a below-the-line technique.
questions.memo: Personal selling deals directly with individual customers, so it is a below-the-line technique.

questions.question: Which of these is an above-the-line technique?
options: A stand at a travel expo
questions.memo: Radio advertising reaches a wide audience through mass media, so it is above-the-line.

questions.question: Which of these is a below-the-line technique?
options: A stand at a travel exhibition or expo
questions.expected: A stand at a travel exhibition or expo
questions.memo: Exhibitions and expos let a business meet potential customers directly, making them below-the-line.

questions.question: A printed _________ is a small folded leaflet handed out to promote a tourism product.
questions.memo: A brochure is printed promotional material that gives information about a product, place or service.

questions.question: True or false: A billboard next to a busy road is an above-the-line technique.
questions.memo: Billboards display a message to a large passing audience through media space, so they are above-the-line.

questions.question: An in-store discount on a holiday package is an example of:
questions.memo: In-store discounts are targeted sales promotions aimed at customers in the shop, so they are below-the-line.

questions.question: Sort each technique into above-the-line or below-the-line.
questions.memo: Mass-media adverts (TV, newspaper, radio) are above-the-line. Direct, targeted methods (personal selling, expos, discounts) are below-the-line.

questions.question: Web-based (online) advertising is usually classed as which type of technique?
options: Above-the-line, because it reaches a wide audience through media
Below-the-line, because it only reaches one person
questions.expected: Above-the-line, because it reaches a wide audience through media
questions.memo: Web-based advertising broadcasts a message to a large online audience, so it is generally treated as above-the-line.

questions.question: True or false: Sponsoring an event is a below-the-line promotional technique.
questions.memo: Promotional sponsorship targets a specific audience at an event, so it is a below-the-line technique.

questions.question: _________ selling is a below-the-line technique where a salesperson deals with a customer one-on-one.
questions.memo: Personal selling is direct, face-to-face contact with a customer, making it a below-the-line method.

questions.question: Which technique would reach the largest general audience at once?
options: A discount handed to a single customer
A poster in one shop window
questions.memo: Television reaches a very large audience at the same time, far more than direct, one-to-one methods.

questions.question: A tour operator wants to reach travel agents who buy tours in bulk. Which is the best-matched technique?
options: A stand at a travel trade expo where agents attend
A poster at a primary school
questions.expected: A stand at a travel trade expo where agents attend
questions.memo: Matching the technique to the audience matters: a travel trade expo reaches exactly the agents the operator wants to sell to.

questions.question: Sort each promotional tool into above-the-line or below-the-line.
questions.memo: Magazine adverts, billboards and web banners reach a mass audience (above-the-line). Sponsorship and discounts target specific customers (below-the-line).

questions.question: True or false: A meander map is a type of printed promotional material.
questions.memo: A meander map is printed promotional material that guides tourists along a route past attractions, shops and restaurants.

questions.question: Why is it important to match a promotional technique to the right audience?
options: The message reaches the people most likely to buy, so the money is well spent
It makes the advert cost as much as possible
It guarantees nobody sees the advert
It removes the need to advertise at all
questions.expected: The message reaches the people most likely to buy, so the money is well spent
questions.memo: Choosing the right technique for the audience means the advertising reaches likely customers, giving better value for money.

questions.question: What is the main difference between above-the-line and below-the-line techniques?
options: Above-the-line uses mass media for a wide audience; below-the-line is direct and targeted
Above-the-line is always free; below-the-line always costs money
Below-the-line can only be used on television
There is no difference between them
questions.expected: Above-the-line uses mass media for a wide audience; below-the-line is direct and targeted
questions.memo: Above-the-line broadcasts to a broad audience through media; below-the-line targets specific customers more directly.

questions.question: _________ and expos are below-the-line events where a business meets potential customers directly.
questions.memo: Exhibitions, shows and expos let businesses connect with customers face-to-face, making them below-the-line techniques.

TOUR.G11.T3.BUDGET.A1.title: The marketing budget
TOUR.G11.T3.BUDGET.A1.description: Identify the costs that belong in a marketing budget (market research, communication costs such as printing, telephone and internet, local and overseas travel and vehicle/flight costs, and personnel costs).
TOUR.G11.T3.BUDGET.A1.strand: Term 3 — Regional tourism, itineraries and marketing
TOUR.G11.T3.BUDGET.A1.recovery_strategy: Group costs under research, communication, travel and personnel, then place one cost at a time.

questions.question: What is a marketing budget?
options: A plan of the money set aside to spend on marketing
The total profit a business makes
The price of a single advert only
The wages of the kitchen staff
questions.expected: A plan of the money set aside to spend on marketing
questions.memo: A marketing budget plans how much money will be spent on marketing activities and what it will be spent on.

questions.question: Which of these is a marketing cost that belongs in a marketing budget?
options: Paying the electricity bill for the storeroom
questions.memo: Market research is a marketing cost. Kitchen, storeroom and vehicle-repair costs are operating costs, not marketing costs.

questions.question: _________ costs in a marketing budget include printing, telephone and internet.
questions.memo: Communication costs cover printing, telephone, fax and internet — the ways a business communicates its marketing.

questions.question: True or false: Travel costs for marketing trips belong in the marketing budget.
questions.memo: Local and overseas travel to promote the business — including vehicle and flight costs — are part of the marketing budget.

questions.question: Which of these is a marketing cost?
options: Buying bedsheets for the guest rooms
questions.memo: Printing promotional brochures and flyers is a communication (marketing) cost. The others are general operating costs.

questions.question: What are personnel costs in a marketing budget?
options: The wages and salaries of the marketing staff
The cost of the building's rent
The price of the food served to guests
The cost of fuel for the tour bus
questions.expected: The wages and salaries of the marketing staff
questions.memo: Personnel costs are the wages and salaries paid to the people who do the marketing work.

questions.question: Market _________ is the cost of finding out what customers want and how to reach them.
questions.memo: Market research gathers information about customers and the market, and its cost is part of the marketing budget.

questions.question: True or false: The cost of food for the restaurant kitchen is a marketing cost.
questions.memo: Kitchen food is an operating cost of running the restaurant, not a marketing cost.

questions.question: Which is an example of a communication cost?
options: The telephone and internet bill for the marketing office
The cost of the guest beds
The fuel for the airport shuttle
questions.expected: The telephone and internet bill for the marketing office
questions.memo: Telephone and internet costs are communication costs used to market and reach customers.

questions.question: Sort each marketing cost into the correct category.

items.text: Flights to an overseas travel expo
Vehicle costs for a local promotion tour

questions.memo: Surveys and studying customers are research; printing and internet are communication; flights and vehicle costs are travel.

questions.question: Which is an example of a travel cost in a marketing budget?
options: Flights for staff to promote the business at an overseas expo
The cost of printing a brochure
questions.expected: Flights for staff to promote the business at an overseas expo
questions.memo: Travel costs include flights and vehicle costs for staff to market the business locally and overseas.

questions.question: True or false: A marketing budget helps a business plan and control its marketing spending.
questions.memo: A budget sets out planned spending in advance, helping the business control costs and avoid overspending.

questions.question: _________ costs are the wages and salaries paid to the marketing team.
questions.memo: Personnel costs are the staff wages and salaries needed to carry out the marketing.

questions.question: Why does a tourism business prepare a marketing budget?
options: To plan and control how much is spent on marketing
To make marketing as expensive as possible
To replace the need for any staff
questions.expected: To plan and control how much is spent on marketing
questions.memo: A marketing budget plans spending in advance so the business can control costs and get the best value from its marketing.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a marketing cost?
options: Buying a new oven for the kitchen
Travel to a tourism trade show
questions.expected: Buying a new oven for the kitchen
questions.memo: A kitchen oven is an operating expense, not a marketing cost. Posters, research and trade-show travel are all marketing costs.

questions.question: Sort each cost by whether it belongs in a marketing budget.
questions.memo: Brochures, research and marketing salaries are marketing costs. Beds and kitchen repairs are general operating costs.

questions.question: True or false: Website and internet costs used for marketing are communication costs.
questions.memo: Internet and website costs used to reach and inform customers are part of the communication costs in a marketing budget.

questions.question: Which is an example of a market research cost?
options: Paying a company to survey what tourists want
questions.expected: Paying a company to survey what tourists want
questions.memo: Paying for surveys and studies to learn about customers is a market research cost.

questions.question: Staff fly overseas to promote a lodge at an international travel show. Which marketing cost category is this?
questions.memo: Flights and travel to promote the business, locally or overseas, fall under travel costs in the marketing budget.

questions.question: A marketing _________ lists the expected marketing costs so spending can be planned.
questions.memo: A marketing budget is the plan that lists the expected marketing costs, helping the business manage its spending.

TOUR.G11.T3.GDS.A1.title: Global distribution and central reservation systems
TOUR.G11.T3.GDS.A1.description: Explain what a Global Distribution System (GDS) is and what it is used for, name the major GDSs (Amadeus, Galileo, Worldspan), and explain what a Central Reservation System (CRS) is, with a South African example (Micros-Fidelio Opera).
TOUR.G11.T3.GDS.A1.strand: Term 3 — Regional tourism, itineraries and marketing
TOUR.G11.T3.GDS.A1.caps_topic: Communication and customer care — global distribution systems
TOUR.G11.T3.GDS.A1.recovery_strategy: Contrast a worldwide GDS that links many suppliers with a single property's CRS, then name examples of each.

questions.question: What is a Global Distribution System (GDS)?
options: A worldwide computer system that links travel suppliers with travel agents
A single hotel's own booking diary
questions.expected: A worldwide computer system that links travel suppliers with travel agents
questions.memo: A GDS is a worldwide computer network that connects travel agents to airlines, hotels and car-hire companies so they can check availability and book.

questions.question: What does GDS stand for?
questions.memo: GDS stands for Global Distribution System — a worldwide network used to distribute and book travel products.

questions.question: Amadeus is an example of a _________.
questions.memo: Amadeus is one of the major Global Distribution Systems, along with Galileo and Worldspan.

questions.question: True or false: A GDS lets travel agents book flights, hotels and car hire from suppliers around the world.
questions.memo: A GDS gives agents access to many suppliers worldwide, so they can check availability and make bookings across flights, hotels and car hire.

questions.question: Which of these is a major Global Distribution System?
questions.memo: Galileo is a major GDS. Metrorail is a train service, SAHRA a heritage body and Retosa a regional tourism organisation.

questions.question: What is a Central Reservation System (CRS)?
options: A system that manages the reservations of a single property or company
A worldwide network linking all travel agents
questions.expected: A system that manages the reservations of a single property or company
questions.memo: A CRS handles bookings for one property or chain (such as a hotel), managing its own availability and reservations.

questions.question: CRS stands for Central _________ System.
questions.memo: CRS stands for Central Reservation System, used to manage a property's bookings centrally.

questions.question: True or false: Micros-Fidelio Opera is an example of a central reservation system used in South Africa.
questions.memo: Micros-Fidelio Opera is a central reservation/property management system widely used by hotels in South Africa.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a GDS and a CRS?
options: A GDS links many suppliers worldwide; a CRS manages one property's own bookings
A GDS is for a single hotel; a CRS is worldwide
They are exactly the same system
A GDS is a currency and a CRS is an airline
questions.expected: A GDS links many suppliers worldwide; a CRS manages one property's own bookings
questions.memo: A GDS is a global network connecting many suppliers and agents; a CRS handles the reservations of a single property or chain.

questions.question: Sort each system into GDS or CRS.
questions.memo: Amadeus, Galileo and Worldspan are global distribution systems. Micros-Fidelio Opera and a single hotel's booking system are central reservation systems.

questions.question: Who mainly uses a Global Distribution System?
options: Travel agents booking travel for their customers
questions.expected: Travel agents booking travel for their customers
questions.memo: Travel agents use a GDS to search availability and book flights, hotels and car hire for their clients.

questions.question: True or false: Worldspan is a Global Distribution System.
questions.memo: Worldspan is one of the major Global Distribution Systems, along with Amadeus and Galileo.

questions.question: A GDS connects travel _________ to many suppliers so they can make bookings.
questions.memo: A GDS links travel agents to suppliers worldwide, letting them check availability and book on behalf of customers.

questions.question: What is a benefit of using a GDS?
options: Agents can see live availability and book many suppliers in one place
It removes the need for any travel suppliers
It only works for one hotel at a time
It makes booking slower and harder
questions.expected: Agents can see live availability and book many suppliers in one place
questions.memo: A GDS shows real-time availability across many suppliers and lets agents book it all in one system, saving time.

questions.question: Galileo is an example of which kind of system?
options: A central reservation system for one hotel
questions.memo: Galileo is a major GDS used by travel agents to book travel from suppliers worldwide.

questions.question: Sort each statement by whether it describes a GDS or a CRS.
questions.memo: A GDS links many suppliers worldwide for travel agents; a CRS manages the reservations of a single property, such as with Micros-Fidelio Opera.

questions.question: True or false: A central reservation system handles the bookings of a single hotel or hotel chain.
questions.memo: A CRS manages reservations for one property or chain, keeping its availability and bookings in order.

questions.question: Which products can a travel agent typically book through a GDS?
questions.memo: A GDS gives access to a wide range of travel products — flights, accommodation and car hire — from many suppliers.

questions.question: What is a benefit of a CRS for a hotel?
options: It helps the hotel manage its own room availability and reservations
It lets the hotel fly its own aircraft
It sets the country's exchange rates
It protects the country's heritage sites
questions.expected: It helps the hotel manage its own room availability and reservations
questions.memo: A CRS lets a hotel keep track of its rooms and bookings in one central system, avoiding double-bookings and confusion.

questions.question: The 'G' in GDS stands for _________, meaning the system operates worldwide.
questions.memo: The 'G' stands for Global, because a GDS connects suppliers and agents across the whole world.

TOUR.G11.T4.CUSTCARE.A1.title: Customer care for foreign tourists
TOUR.G11.T4.CUSTCARE.A1.description: Explain how foreign tourists should be treated and assisted, why their traditions, customs and behaviour must be respected, ways to communicate across cultures, and how excellent customer care benefits South Africa's tourism industry.
TOUR.G11.T4.CUSTCARE.A1.strand: Term 4 — Customer care, quality service and careers
TOUR.G11.T4.CUSTCARE.A1.caps_topic: Communication and customer care — customer care for foreign tourists
TOUR.G11.T4.CUSTCARE.A1.recovery_strategy: Role-play helping a visitor from a different culture, then identify the respectful, helpful choice in each case.

questions.question: Why is good customer care for foreign tourists important to South Africa?
options: Happy visitors are more likely to return and recommend the country to others
It guarantees flights are never delayed
It removes the need for any tourism marketing
It makes the rand stronger overnight
questions.expected: Happy visitors are more likely to return and recommend the country to others
questions.memo: Excellent customer care leaves tourists with a good impression, so they return and tell others, boosting South Africa's tourism industry.

questions.question: Why should staff respect the traditions and customs of foreign visitors?
options: Visitors feel welcome and comfortable, which improves their stay
It allows staff to ignore the visitors completely
It makes the visitors leave sooner
It has no effect on the visitor's experience
questions.expected: Visitors feel welcome and comfortable, which improves their stay
questions.memo: Respecting visitors' customs shows courtesy and makes them feel valued, improving their experience and impression of South Africa.

questions.question: Speaking clearly and using simple language helps when communicating with visitors who speak a different _________.
questions.memo: Many foreign visitors speak a different language, so clear, simple speech (and visual aids) helps them understand.

questions.question: True or false: A friendly, helpful welcome makes foreign tourists more likely to recommend South Africa to others.
questions.memo: Warm, helpful service creates a good impression, so visitors are more likely to return and recommend the destination.

questions.question: A foreign tourist looks lost in the airport. What is the best customer care response?
options: Offer friendly help and clear directions
Tell them to figure it out themselves
questions.expected: Offer friendly help and clear directions
questions.memo: Good customer care means noticing when a visitor needs help and offering it warmly and clearly.

questions.question: Why is it useful for tourism staff to learn a few words of other languages?
options: It helps visitors feel welcome and eases communication
It guarantees the visitor will spend more money
It replaces the need to be polite
questions.expected: It helps visitors feel welcome and eases communication
questions.memo: Even a few words in a visitor's language shows effort and respect, making communication smoother and the welcome warmer.

questions.question: Treating visitors from all cultures with _________ helps them enjoy their stay in South Africa.
questions.memo: Respect for visitors' cultures and needs is at the heart of good customer care and makes for a positive experience.

questions.question: True or false: Every foreign visitor expects exactly the same service as a local resident.
questions.memo: Visitors come from different cultures with different customs and expectations, so good staff adapt their service rather than assuming everyone is the same.

questions.question: Compare how two staff members assist a foreign tourist, then judge each statement.

source_a.text: The guide greeted the visitors warmly, spoke slowly and clearly, learned how to say hello in their language, and patiently answered all their questions.
source_a.provenance: Notes from a tour company's customer care training

source_b.text: The clerk sighed at the visitors, spoke very fast, rolled his eyes at their questions, and walked away before they had finished.
source_b.provenance: A complaint posted on a travel review website

statements.text: Involves a member of staff helping tourists

questions.memo: Source A is warm, patient and respectful (excellent care); Source B is rude and dismissive (poor service). Both involve staff and tourists; neither mentions currency.

questions.question: Sort each action by whether it is good or poor customer care for foreign tourists.

items.text: Being rude about a visitor's accent
Rushing visitors and refusing to answer questions

questions.memo: Warmth, patience and respect are good care. Ignoring, mocking or rushing visitors is poor care.

questions.question: How can the tourism industry benefit from excellent customer care for foreign tourists?
options: Visitors return and recommend South Africa, bringing more tourism income
It causes tourists to avoid the country
It reduces the number of jobs in tourism
It has no effect on the industry
questions.expected: Visitors return and recommend South Africa, bringing more tourism income
questions.memo: Great care leads to repeat visits and word-of-mouth recommendations, growing tourism and the income and jobs it brings.

questions.question: True or false: Being patient with visitors who do not speak the local language is part of good customer care.
questions.memo: Patience helps visitors who struggle with the language feel respected and understood, which is part of good care.

questions.question: Using pictures, maps or simple gestures can help when there is a _________ barrier with a visitor.
questions.memo: When words are hard to understand, visual aids and gestures help bridge a language barrier.

questions.question: A visitor's custom is different from your own. What is the respectful response?
options: Accept the difference politely and adapt your service
Tell them their custom is wrong
questions.expected: Accept the difference politely and adapt your service
questions.memo: Respecting differences means accepting them politely and adjusting service, not judging or mocking the visitor.

questions.question: What is a likely result of rude or unhelpful service towards foreign tourists?
options: They may complain, give bad reviews and not return
They will definitely recommend the country
It increases the number of return visits
questions.expected: They may complain, give bad reviews and not return
questions.memo: Poor service drives visitors away and damages reputation through bad reviews, harming the tourism industry.

questions.question: Sort each behaviour by whether it shows respect for a visitor's culture.

items.text: Learning a polite greeting in the visitor's language
Telling a visitor their customs are strange

questions.memo: Learning greetings, accepting differences and listening are respectful. Mocking or judging customs is disrespectful.

questions.question: True or false: Good customer care can encourage repeat visits and positive word-of-mouth.
questions.memo: Visitors who are well cared for tend to come back and recommend the destination to friends and family.

questions.question: A tour guide notices a visitor seems unsure about a local custom. What is the best approach?
options: Kindly explain the custom so the visitor feels at ease
Embarrass the visitor in front of the group
Insist the visitor follow it without explanation
questions.expected: Kindly explain the custom so the visitor feels at ease
questions.memo: Helpfully explaining local customs puts visitors at ease and helps them enjoy and respect the experience.

questions.question: Which is an example of helping a foreign visitor feel welcome?
options: Greeting them warmly and offering assistance
Speaking to them in a harsh tone
questions.expected: Greeting them warmly and offering assistance
questions.memo: A warm greeting and an offer of help make a visitor feel welcome and valued.

questions.question: Excellent customer care helps build South Africa's _________ as a welcoming tourist destination.
questions.memo: Consistently good care builds the country's reputation, attracting more visitors over time.

TOUR.G11.T4.COMPLAINTS.A1.title: Customer complaints
TOUR.G11.T4.COMPLAINTS.A1.description: Recognise channels for complaints (in person, telephone, written), the value of complaints as a chance to improve, the six steps for handling a verbal complaint, and how to handle criticism in a mature, constructive way.
TOUR.G11.T4.COMPLAINTS.A1.strand: Term 4 — Customer care, quality service and careers
TOUR.G11.T4.COMPLAINTS.A1.caps_topic: Communication and customer care — customer complaints
TOUR.G11.T4.COMPLAINTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Memorise the six steps in order (listen, ask, apologise, solve, offer, thank), then practise sequencing one complaint at a time.

questions.question: Why can a customer complaint be valuable to a business?
options: It shows the business what to fix and improve
It always means the business should close
It proves the customer is wrong
It has no use at all
questions.expected: It shows the business what to fix and improve
questions.memo: A complaint is an opportunity: it points out a problem so the business can fix it and improve its service.

questions.question: What is the FIRST step when handling a verbal customer complaint?
options: Listen carefully and let the customer finish
questions.expected: Listen carefully and let the customer finish
questions.memo: The first step is to listen carefully and let the customer say everything, so they feel heard and you understand the problem.

questions.question: When handling a complaint you should apologise without _________ the customer.
questions.memo: Apologise sincerely without blaming the customer; this calms the situation and shows you take the problem seriously.

questions.question: True or false: A complaint can be made in person, by telephone, or in writing.
questions.memo: Customers may complain verbally (in person or by phone) or in writing (letters, emails, SMSs or website reviews).

questions.question: Place the six steps for handling a verbal complaint in the correct order.

items.text: Listen carefully and let them finish
Ask questions in a caring way
Thank the customer for telling you

questions.memo: The six steps are: listen, ask, apologise, solve, offer something, and thank the customer.

questions.question: After listening, what should you do next in the six-step process?
options: Ask questions in a caring and concerned manner
Tell the customer they are mistaken
questions.expected: Ask questions in a caring and concerned manner
questions.memo: After listening, ask caring questions to fully understand the problem before solving it.

questions.question: Offering an upgrade, a free product or a discount is which step in handling a complaint?
questions.memo: Offering something extra — an upgrade, free product, discount or refund — helps make up for the problem.

questions.question: True or false: The last step in handling a verbal complaint is to thank the customer for telling you about the problem.
questions.memo: Thanking the customer ends the interaction positively and shows you value their feedback.

questions.question: Which of these is a written form of complaint?
options: An email or a review on a website
A spoken comment at the desk
questions.expected: An email or a review on a website
questions.memo: Written complaints include letters, emails, SMSs and online reviews. Phone calls and in-person comments are verbal.

questions.question: Sort each complaint channel into verbal or written.

items.text: Speaking in person at the desk
A review posted on a website
A complaint made over the counter

questions.memo: Verbal complaints are spoken (in person or by phone). Written complaints are emails, SMSs, letters and online reviews.

questions.question: Why should you solve a customer's problem immediately where possible?
options: It shows you care and stops the problem from getting worse
It is not important to act quickly
questions.expected: It shows you care and stops the problem from getting worse
questions.memo: Acting quickly shows the customer you take their complaint seriously and prevents the situation from escalating.

questions.question: True or false: Complaints should be treated as an opportunity to improve the business.
questions.memo: Each complaint highlights something to fix, helping the business improve and keep customers happy.

questions.question: Handling criticism in a _________ way means staying calm and not taking it personally.
questions.memo: Mature handling of criticism means staying calm, listening and using the feedback to improve, rather than reacting badly.

questions.question: What is constructive criticism?
options: Feedback meant to help you improve
Rude comments meant only to hurt
questions.expected: Feedback meant to help you improve
questions.memo: Constructive criticism is helpful feedback that points out problems so they can be fixed and improved.

questions.question: A customer is upset about a cold meal. Following the six steps, what should you do before solving the problem?
options: Listen, ask caring questions and apologise
Immediately argue that the meal was fine
questions.expected: Listen, ask caring questions and apologise
questions.memo: The steps before solving are: listen, ask, then apologise. Only after that do you solve the problem and offer something.

questions.question: Sort each action by whether it is a good or poor way to handle a complaint.
questions.memo: Listening, apologising and solving quickly are good. Arguing, ignoring and blaming are poor.

questions.question: True or false: You should thank a customer for complaining, because it helps you improve.
questions.memo: Thanking the customer recognises that their feedback is valuable and helps the business get better.

questions.question: Why is it important to stay calm when a customer is angry?
options: Staying calm helps settle the situation and solve the problem
It encourages the customer to shout louder
It lets you avoid helping them
questions.expected: Staying calm helps settle the situation and solve the problem
questions.memo: A calm, professional response helps defuse anger and makes it easier to find a solution.

questions.question: What is an example of 'offering the customer something' after a complaint?
options: Giving a free upgrade or a discount
questions.expected: Giving a free upgrade or a discount
questions.memo: Offering an upgrade, free product, discount or refund helps make up for the problem and keep the customer's goodwill.

questions.question: A complaint is an _________ for a business to improve its service.
questions.memo: Seen positively, a complaint is an opportunity to learn what is wrong and put it right.

TOUR.G11.T4.QUALITY.A1.title: Managing quality service
TOUR.G11.T4.QUALITY.A1.description: Identify the strategies companies use to achieve and maintain quality service (performance management, quality-control checks, customer surveys, team and peer reviews, in-service training) and explain how service in one sector affects service in another.
TOUR.G11.T4.QUALITY.A1.strand: Term 4 — Customer care, quality service and careers
TOUR.G11.T4.QUALITY.A1.caps_topic: Communication and customer care — managing quality service
TOUR.G11.T4.QUALITY.A1.recovery_strategy: Match each strategy to the problem it fixes, then trace how one weak link affects the whole tourism chain.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a customer survey?
options: To find out what customers think so the service can be improved
To increase the price of every product
To replace the need for staff
questions.expected: To find out what customers think so the service can be improved
questions.memo: Customer surveys gather feedback on the service so the business can see what to keep and what to improve.

questions.question: What is the aim of in-service training for staff?
options: To improve staff skills so they deliver better service
To give staff less to do
To lower the quality of service
questions.expected: To improve staff skills so they deliver better service
questions.memo: In-service training develops staff skills and knowledge while they work, helping them give better quality service.

questions.question: Regular quality-control _________ help a business check that its service meets the required standard.
questions.memo: Quality-control checks regularly test the service against the standard, so problems are caught and fixed.

questions.question: True or false: Poor service in one tourism sector can harm the reputation of others in the chain.
questions.memo: Tourism sectors are linked: a bad experience at the airport, for example, can spoil a tour operator's whole package in the visitor's eyes.

questions.question: What is performance management?
options: Setting standards and reviewing how well staff meet them
Letting staff do whatever they like
Reducing the quality of the product
questions.expected: Setting standards and reviewing how well staff meet them
questions.memo: Performance management sets clear standards and regularly reviews staff against them, helping maintain quality service.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by choosing the strong supporting points.
questions.thesis: Quality service in one tourism sector affects the experience in other sectors.

pool.text: A delayed, rude airport experience can ruin a visitor's view of the whole trip
Tourists judge a destination by every link in the chain, from transport to lodging
A great tour can be spoilt by one poor hotel or transfer

questions.memo: The strong points all show how one weak link affects the whole tourism experience. The red herrings are true but irrelevant to the link between sectors.

questions.question: A _________ review is when team members or peers give each other feedback to improve service.
questions.memo: Team and peer reviews let colleagues give each other helpful feedback, supporting better quality service.

questions.question: True or false: Customer surveys are one way to measure and improve service quality.
questions.memo: Surveys collect customer feedback, which the business uses to measure satisfaction and improve quality.

questions.question: How does an airport's poor service affect a tour operator?
options: It can give the tourist a bad first impression of the whole trip
It has no effect on the tour operator
It improves the tour operator's reputation
It only affects the airline's profit
questions.expected: It can give the tourist a bad first impression of the whole trip
questions.memo: Because sectors are linked, a poor airport experience colours the tourist's view of everything that follows, including the tour.

questions.question: Sort each item by whether it is a quality-service strategy.
questions.memo: Surveys, training, quality checks and peer reviews are strategies. Ignoring feedback and letting standards drop are not.

questions.question: Why do companies use several quality-service strategies together?
options: Each strategy checks a different part, helping keep service consistently high
questions.expected: Each strategy checks a different part, helping keep service consistently high
questions.memo: Using surveys, training, checks and reviews together covers different angles, keeping service consistently high.

questions.question: True or false: In-service training takes place while staff continue to do their jobs.
questions.memo: In-service training develops staff skills on the job, without them leaving work for long periods.

questions.question: Setting clear standards and reviewing staff against them is called performance _________.
questions.memo: Performance management sets standards and reviews how well staff meet them, supporting quality service.

questions.question: Why is consistent quality service important in tourism?
options: Tourists expect good service at every step, and one weak link can spoil the trip
It does not matter as long as one part is good
Only the hotel needs to be good
Quality has no effect on tourists
questions.expected: Tourists expect good service at every step, and one weak link can spoil the trip
questions.memo: A trip is a chain of experiences; tourists notice every link, so consistent quality across all sectors matters.

questions.question: Which is an example of using customer feedback to improve quality?
options: Reading survey results and fixing the problems raised
Throwing away all the survey forms
questions.expected: Reading survey results and fixing the problems raised
questions.memo: Acting on survey feedback — fixing the problems customers raise — is how feedback improves quality.

questions.question: Match each quality strategy to what it mainly does.
questions.memo: Surveys and peer reviews gather feedback; training builds skills; quality-control and performance reviews check standards.

questions.question: True or false: Good service from a tour guide can be undone by a rude transfer driver.
questions.memo: Because the trip is a chain, one poor link (a rude driver) can spoil the overall experience even when other parts are excellent.

questions.question: What does a quality-control check involve?
options: Inspecting the service against a set standard to catch problems
Closing the business for the day
questions.expected: Inspecting the service against a set standard to catch problems
questions.memo: Quality-control checks compare the actual service to the required standard so problems can be spotted and corrected.

questions.question: Why do tourism businesses depend on each other for quality?
options: A tourist's overall experience depends on every business in the chain doing well
Only one business in the chain matters
questions.expected: A tourist's overall experience depends on every business in the chain doing well
questions.memo: Transport, accommodation, attractions and guides all link together; the tourist judges the whole, so each business affects the others.

questions.question: Gathering staff feedback through team and _________ reviews helps maintain quality service.
questions.memo: Team and peer reviews let colleagues share feedback and learn from each other, supporting consistent quality.

TOUR.G11.T4.CAREERS.A1.title: Job and career opportunities in tourism
TOUR.G11.T4.CAREERS.A1.description: Identify job and career opportunities across the tourism sectors and sub-sectors (transport, hospitality, attractions, gaming, conservation, sport and recreation, events and conferences, tourism services and the travel trade).
TOUR.G11.T4.CAREERS.A1.strand: Term 4 — Customer care, quality service and careers
TOUR.G11.T4.CAREERS.A1.caps_topic: Tourism sectors — job and career opportunities in tourism
TOUR.G11.T4.CAREERS.A1.recovery_strategy: Match each job to the sector it belongs to, one career at a time.

questions.question: A tour guide works in which tourism sector?
questions.memo: Tour guides work in tourism services, helping visitors experience attractions and destinations.

questions.question: A chef in a hotel restaurant works in which sector?
questions.memo: A chef works in the hospitality sector, specifically food and beverage, preparing meals for guests.

questions.question: A game ranger in a national park works in the _________ sector.
questions.memo: Game rangers work in conservation, protecting wildlife and natural areas that attract tourists.

questions.question: True or false: A pilot works in the transport sector of tourism.
questions.memo: Pilots work in the transport sector, moving tourists by air between destinations.

questions.question: Which job belongs to the events and conferences sector?
questions.memo: A conference organiser works in the events and conferences sector, planning and running business and special events.

questions.question: A travel agent who books holidays for clients works in which sector?
questions.memo: Travel agents work in the travel trade, arranging flights, accommodation and tours for customers.

questions.question: A receptionist at a hotel works in the _________ sector.
questions.memo: Hotel receptionists work in the hospitality (accommodation) sector, welcoming and assisting guests.

questions.question: True or false: A casino dealer works in the gaming and lotteries sub-sector of tourism.
questions.memo: Casino staff such as dealers work in the gaming and lotteries part of the leisure and entertainment sector.

questions.question: Which of these is a tourism career in the transport sector?
questions.memo: A coach driver works in transport, moving tourists by road between destinations.

questions.question: Sort each job into the correct tourism sector.
questions.memo: Cabin crew and coach drivers are transport; chefs and receptionists are hospitality; rangers and museum guides are attractions/conservation.

questions.question: A tour operator who designs and sells package tours works in which sector?
questions.memo: Tour operators work in the travel trade, putting together and selling tour packages.

questions.question: True or false: A scuba-diving instructor at a coastal resort works in the sport and recreation part of tourism.
questions.memo: Activity instructors such as scuba-diving instructors work in the sport and recreation/leisure part of tourism.

questions.question: A waiter serving guests in a restaurant works in the food and _________ sector.
questions.memo: Waiters work in food and beverage, part of the hospitality sector, serving meals and drinks to guests.

questions.question: Which job is found in the accommodation part of the hospitality sector?
questions.memo: Housekeepers work in accommodation (hospitality), keeping guest rooms clean and comfortable.

questions.question: An events manager planning a large conference works in which sector?
questions.memo: Events managers work in the events and conferences sector, organising meetings, conferences and functions.

questions.question: Sort each job into the correct sector.
questions.memo: Travel agents and tour operators are travel trade; conference organisers and events managers are events; rangers and wardens are conservation.

questions.question: True or false: A museum curator works in the tourism attractions sector.
questions.memo: Museum curators work in the attractions sector, caring for and presenting collections that tourists visit.
